title: "This day I have perfected"
hook: at Arafah the verse comes: this day I have perfected your religion (5:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell sermon on the plain of Arafah: every life sacred, and no Arab above a non-Arab except by goodness, by taqwa. Your line was no one above another.

On the day of Arafah, during that same Hajj, a Friday that year, a verse came down to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, twenty-three years after the first revelation in the cave. It's in the fifth surah, tucked into the middle of a passage about food. You know the feeling it names: something you've worked on for years is finally done. The last brick. The final page. You step back and look at it whole for the first time. It's joy, and something quieter too, because a thing that's finished also means a season is over.
screen: `ARAFAH, ON A FRIDAY.` → `TWENTY-THREE YEARS AFTER THE CAVE.` → `THE LAST BRICK.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse reads: "This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion AL-ISLAM." Three verbs, in order: perfected, completed, chosen. The Arabic behind perfected is akmaltu, from kamal, wholeness, the thing lacking nothing. Muslims understand the verse to mean the religion was now complete: its core teaching, its worship and its law were in place, and nothing essential would be added after the Prophet. That's one reason the sunnah matters so much, and why Muslim scholars are careful about new additions to worship. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a striking conversation about this verse. A Jewish man told the caliph 'Umar: there's a verse in your book that, if it had come to us, we would have made that day a festival. 'Umar asked which one, and the man recited this verse. And 'Umar said: I know the day and the place it came down. It was at Arafah, on a Friday. As if to say: we already hold that day as a great one. A common mistake: this is not universally counted as the last verse revealed. Many scholars say a few other verses came after it, and they discuss which was truly last. What it marks is the whole being complete. And some companions heard sadness in it too. If the work is complete, the one who brought it may not stay much longer. Eighty-some days later, he was gone.
screen: `PERFECTED, COMPLETED, CHOSEN.` · `AKMALTU — NOTHING LACKING.` · `'UMAR: I KNOW THE DAY AND THE PLACE.` · `COMPLETE, NOT NECESSARILY LAST.` · then, large: `COMPLETED.`

segments.voice: At Uhud the line was hold the hill, staying at your post; today is the other half, the moment the work is done. Think of one small thing you've left almost done, the email drafted, the drawer half sorted, the thank-you you meant to send, and picture it complete: sent, sorted, said, whole. If you pray, you can give thanks for something in your life that is already complete.
Akmaltu. I have perfected — the verb in the verse at Arafah, from kamal, wholeness, telling Muslims their religion was complete. Today's word.
Your line: completed. Joy, and a quiet sense that a season is ending. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims hold the day of Arafah as one of the holiest of the year; many who are not on Hajj fast that day, and 5:3 is often recited to explain that the religion was completed in the Prophet's lifetime.
